## The Whole Module in One Slide {.smaller}

The arc, in the order it happened:

| Lectures | What you learned to do |
|---|---|
| **1-7** | See data, and build something a stakeholder can read |
| **8-11** | Cause the data to exist, lawfully, and get it back out |
| **12-17** | Compute with it, and distrust it |
| **18-22** | Say what it is worth and what it proves |
| **23-24** | Put it in front of someone who pays |

. . .

**Blocks 2 and 3 are deliberately in that order.** You had to be handed somebody
else's clean dataset before building your own was worth anything.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Present an analytics finding to a non-technical audience
- Defend your methodology under questioning
- Reflect on the limits of your own analysis

# 1. Presenting

## Present in the Opposite Order

You did the work as: data → cleaning → analysis → finding.

. . .

**You present it as: finding → evidence → method → caveats.**

. . .

Nobody in the room wants the chronology. They want to know what you concluded,
and then, only if they are interested, how you got there.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The narrative order from Lecture 7 said the same thing about a dashboard:
introduction, analysis, conclusion, with the conclusion doing real work. A
presentation compresses it further, because you can be interrupted.
:::

## Ten Minutes, Three Points

A client remembers **three things**, and that number does not go up if you talk
for longer.

. . .

So decide, in advance, what the three are. Everything else on your slides is
evidence for one of them or it comes out.

. . .

**A rough shape for ten minutes:**

| Minutes | Content |
|---|---|
| 0-1 | The finding, stated plainly |
| 1-6 | Three points, with one visual each |
| 6-8 | How you know, including what you excluded |
| 8-10 | What you would do next, and what would change your mind |

## Presenting Uncertainty

The hardest skill in this module, and the one that separates an analyst from a
dashboard operator.

. . .

- **Ranges, not points.** "Between 4% and 9%, most likely around 6%" is more
  useful and more honest than "6.3%"
- **Name the sample size** in the sentence, not the footnote. "Across 38
  sessions" changes how a number is heard, which is the point
- **Say what would change your answer.** It converts a hedge into a plan

. . .

**"We do not know yet, and here is what it would take to find out" is a strong
answer.** "6.3%" from 38 sessions is a weak one that sounds strong.

## Anticipating the Hard Question

Write down the three questions you least want to be asked. Rehearse the answers
out loud.

. . .

The usual three, on this module's work:

1. *"How many people is that actually?"*
2. *"What did you exclude, and why?"*
3. *"Would you spend your own money on this?"*

. . .

**You have the answers.** They are in your cleaning log, your consent-bias note,
and your contribution calculation. What you need is to have said them once before
somebody asks.

# 2. Assessment Briefing

## Assignment 2 {.smaller}

**Your website plus an analytics report**, due mid-April, 25% of the module.

The report covers your own site, your own traffic, and your own measurement
decisions:

- What the site was for, and the success statement you wrote in Lecture 8
- What you measured, and why those events
- What the data says, with the honest sample sizes
- What you cleaned, and what that cost you
- What you would do next

. . .

**The in-class test at the end of April covers the module's concepts**, not the
tools' menus.

## How This Is Marked {.smaller}

The principle, stated in Lecture 1 and applied throughout:

> **Documented judgement beats undocumented certainty.**

. . .

Concretely, in this report:

- A caveat you raise yourself costs you nothing. The same caveat found by your
  marker costs you a lot
- A small number reported honestly scores above a large number you cannot defend
- "I excluded these 87 rows because..." is worth more than a clean-looking table
  with no history

. . .

**There is no version of this where the best mark goes to the most impressive
figure.**

# 3. Presentations

## Student Presentations {background="#43464B"}

Ten minutes each, plus five for questions.

For every presentation you watch, answer three questions in writing:

1. What was the single finding?
2. What evidence supported it?
3. What was the biggest **unstated** assumption?

. . .

Hand your three answers to the presenter afterwards. The third one is the gift.

# 4. Synthesis

## What This Module Was Actually About

Not GA4. Not Tableau. Not Python.

. . .

All three will change, and two of them will probably be replaced inside your
career. GA4 replaced Universal Analytics, which replaced Urchin.

. . .

**The transferable skill is deciding what is worth measuring, and being honest
about what the measurement can support.** Everything else was a delivery vehicle
for that.

## The Three Ideas Worth Keeping {.smaller}

1. **"What decision would change if this number were different?"** From Lecture 1,
   and the fastest way to strip a dashboard down to what matters
2. **Say the grain out loud.** From Lecture 2, and the source of most wrong
   numbers in marketing
3. **Documented judgement beats undocumented certainty.** From everywhere, and
   the only one of the three that is about character rather than technique

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
If you remember nothing else from twenty-four sessions, these three will still
make you better than most people in the room.
:::

# 5. AI and What You Submit

## Disclosure, One More Time

Every submission carries three sentences:

1. Which tools you used
2. What you used them for
3. What you changed after checking

. . .

**Nobody loses marks for using AI.** People lose marks for numbers they cannot
defend, and that was true before any of this existed.

## The Question You Will Be Asked

In the viva, in a job interview, and in every meeting after that:

> **"How do you know that is right?"**

. . .

**Acceptable answers name a check**: a figure reconciled against GA4, a case
computed by hand, a row count that did not change across a join, a total that
matches the source.

. . .

**Unacceptable answers name a tool.** "Python calculated it", "the agent ran it",
"it is what the dashboard says". None of those is a check, and everyone senior
enough to matter knows it.

## What Actually Transfers

Lecture 12 opened this thread: you will hand more execution to the machine as you
become more able to check it.

. . .

That is now the job description. The typing is commoditised; **the checking is
not**, because the checking requires knowing what the number is supposed to mean
and what would make it wrong.

. . .

**Which is what the last twenty-four sessions were for.**

## Where to Go Next {.smaller}

**Certifications worth the time**

- Google Analytics Certification, and the Analytics Academy courses
- Tableau Desktop Specialist
- Google Cloud, if BigQuery interested you

**Reading**

- Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, free online
- McKinney, *Python for Data Analysis*
- Kohavi, Tang and Xu, *Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments*

**Practice**

- Keep the site running and the property collecting. In a year it is a portfolio
  with real data behind it, which almost no other candidate has
- Tableau Public, as a public body of work
